title: Checkout Got Slow at 14:00
statement: Checkout's p99 jumped from 400 ms to 3 seconds at 14:00, while its p50 stayed at 90 ms. Checkout calls six services. Exercise assumptions: every call carries a request ID; every slow or failed trace is kept; logs from all services are searchable by time and request ID; CPU graphs exist for every server. The team wants to name the slow service in a few minutes. Which first step fits?
examples: A trace shows each service's span with its duration, so the longest span stands out.
constraints: Find which service is slow, not only that checkout is slow.
Prefer the quickest path to the answer.

approaches.name: Open several kept traces of checkouts slower than 3 seconds since 14:00
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Each trace shows every span with its time, so the service where the 3 seconds went stands out, and several traces confirm it is the same one. The request IDs then lead to that service's logs.

approaches.name: Search all services' logs from 14:00 for errors and timeouts
approaches.hint: Read what happened around that time
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Longer: many lines from six services
approaches.why: It can find the cause, especially if the slow service logs timeouts, but without starting from a slow request it means reading many lines from six services, and a slow service may log nothing at all.

approaches.name: Look for the server with the highest CPU
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A service can be slow because it waits on something else, such as a card provider, while its CPU is low; and a busy server may be fine. CPU is a cause to check later, not a way to find the slow step.

title: An SLI for Photo Uploads
statement: A photo app wants an SLI for uploads. Users complain when an upload fails or takes more than 5 seconds. Uploads pass through a load balancer to 8 servers. Exercise assumptions: the load balancer records the result and time of every upload, including those that never reached a server; each server records only the uploads it handled; the team wants one SLI that matches what users feel, measured as close to the users as the existing records allow. Which SLI fits?
examples: An SLI is a share of good events, such as good uploads ÷ all uploads.
constraints: Count both failures and uploads slower than 5 seconds.
Include uploads that never reached a server.

approaches.name: The share of uploads that succeed within 5 seconds, from the load balancer's records
approaches.hint: Good events seen nearest the user
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: It counts both things users complain about, failures and slow uploads, and the load balancer also sees uploads that failed before any server answered.

approaches.name: Two SLIs from the load balancer's records: the share of uploads that succeed, and the share of successful uploads that finish within 5 seconds
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Together they count failures and slow uploads, including uploads that never reached a server, and they show which kind of problem it is. It meets the requirements but gives two numbers to track, against the stated wish for one SLI.

approaches.name: The average upload time
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: An average hides the slow uploads in the tail and ignores failures completely, so it can stay flat while users suffer. It is not a share of good events.

title: When to Wake Someone
statement: An API has an SLO of 99.9% of requests good over 30 days and handles about 50 requests per second. Exercise assumptions: the requirement is to wake an engineer within an hour when a problem would use the whole month's budget within a day, and never for problems the budget can absorb; short blips of a few minutes happen several times a week and fix themselves; the team prefers as few pages as the requirement allows. Which rule fits?
examples: Burn rate = bad share ÷ allowed share; at 30, a 30-day budget is gone in a day.
constraints: Page within an hour when the budget would be gone within a day.
Do not page for problems the budget can absorb.

approaches.name: Page when more than 3% of the last hour's requests are bad
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Pages within an hour of a fast burn
approaches.why: 3% is 30 × the allowed 0.1%, the burn rate that empties the budget in a day. Looking at a full hour fires within an hour for a real problem, while a few-minute blip rarely lifts an hour's share above 3%.

approaches.name: Page when more than 3% of the last 5 minutes' requests are bad
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: It catches every fast burn within the hour, but the self-fixing blips several times a week also pass 3% for 5 minutes, so it wakes people more often than needed, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: Page on every failed request
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The SLO allows 0.1% of about 130 million requests a month, roughly 130,000 failures, to happen without harm. Paging on each one breaks the rule not to page for what the budget can absorb.
